h1: Whisky stones and other chilling tricks
title: Whisky Stones and Chilling Tricks | Craft Beer School
desc: Do whisky stones work? The physics of stones against ice, how cold they really get your drink and better ways to chill whisky in Indian heat.
teaser: Whisky stones chill without water. They also chill far less than you expect. The reason is one number.
standfirst: Soapstone cubes and steel balls promise cold whisky with no dilution. They deliver the second part. Here is why the first part falls short and what else works.
sections: Stones chill without water, but only a little

Whisky stones are cubes of soapstone, granite or stainless steel kept in the freezer and dropped into the glass. They cool the drink and add no water. That is the whole pitch. As far as it goes, it is honest.

The catch is physics. A stone from the freezer cools a whisky far less than the same weight of ice. Once you see why, you can decide whether that matters for the way you drink.
Ice wins because melting soaks up heat

Ice absorbs heat in two steps. First it warms to 0 °C. Then it melts. Melting is the big one: about 334 joules per gram, the same energy that would heat a gram of water by roughly 80 °C. A stone has no melting step. It only soaks up heat as its own temperature rises.

Stone and steel also hold less heat per gram than water. Soapstone holds roughly a quarter as much and steel roughly an eighth. Put those together and the gap is large. In a rough kitchen calculation, three small soapstone cubes from a -18 °C freezer bring a 60 ml pour at 30 °C down to around 20 °C once the glass has taken its share. Two ice cubes take the same pour into single figures, with water to show for it.
What stones are actually good for

Twenty degrees sounds like failure until you remember that it is close to the temperature most tasting guides recommend. In an Indian room at 30 °C or more, a neat whisky warms in the glass and the alcohol starts to dominate the nose. Stones pull it back to a cellar-like temperature without changing the strength.

So stones suit the drinker who likes whisky neat and wants it a little cooler, not cold. If you want an icy drink, stones will disappoint you. If you want a neat malt that does not turn hot and spirity on a summer evening, they do a fair job.
Handle them like kit, not jewellery

Stones need a little care. Wash them after use and dry them fully before they go back in the freezer. Store them in a sealed bag or box, because porous stone picks up freezer smells and passes them to the next drink. Lower them in with a spoon or tongs. A cold stone dropped into a thin glass can chip it.

Steel versions sometimes contain a sealed liquid core to hold more cold. Bin any that are dented or leaking. Never let anyone bite down on one, which sounds obvious until it happens at the end of a long evening.

The simplest is the glass itself. Ten minutes in the freezer and a thick tumbler will keep a pour cool for a good while. You can also keep the bottle in the fridge. A 40% spirit freezes well below the -18 °C of a domestic freezer, so even there it stays liquid, though very cold whisky smells of very little.

A single large ice sphere is the middle path: real chill, slow dilution. Some drinkers in India go further and lengthen whisky with chilled coconut water or soda; our piece on coconut water and other Indian mixers covers those. That is a different drink. It is a perfectly good one.
Dilution is not always the enemy

The selling point of stones is that they keep water out of the glass. That is only a benefit if water was the problem. For many whiskies, a little dilution helps. Bottled at 40% or above, the alcohol can numb the nose; a few millilitres of water often lets fruit and cereal notes come forward.

So treat chilling and dilution as two separate dials. Stones let you cool a whisky without turning the second dial. You can still add water yourself, drop by drop, with a pipette or a teaspoon. That gives you more control than ice ever will, which is the real argument for stones. Cask strength whiskies at 55% or more especially benefit from that two-step approach: water first to open them up, then a mild chill to stop the heat of the room taking over.
Measure it once and you will know

Most arguments about whisky stones are guesses. You can settle yours with a probe thermometer from the kitchen drawer.

Pour three 30 ml measures of the same whisky. Add stones to the first, one ice cube to the second and leave the third neat in a frozen glass. After five minutes, write down the temperature of each. Then taste them in order and note which one you would happily pour again. Your own numbers beat any product description.
faqs: They cool whisky without diluting it, but much less than ice does. Ice soaks up a great deal of heat as it melts and stones have no melting step.
Can I keep whisky in the freezer?
Yes. A 40% ABV spirit will not freeze at domestic freezer temperatures. It will smell of very little until it warms up in the glass.
Are steel whisky stones better than soapstone?
Steel holds less heat per gram than soapstone, though designs with a sealed liquid core make up some of the gap. Either way, the chill is mild.
